subject: physics
question_text: State the second law of thermodynamics.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Very Short Answer Question 15 (printed p.125). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the Clausius statement (no process transfers heat from a colder body to a hotter body with no other effect) and the Kelvin-Planck statement (no engine working in a cycle converts heat from a single reservoir entirely into work) are the two standard, equivalent statements of the second law of thermodynamics.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Clausius statement
lines: Clausius statement: heat does not flow on
its own from a colder body to a hotter
body. It flows that way only when external
work is done on the system.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that heat does not flow from cold to hot on its own.
steps.why: The second law adds a rule the first law does not: it fixes the direction heat can flow without outside help.
common_mistakes: Leaving out "on its own". Heat does flow from cold to hot when work is supplied, as in a refrigerator.
Writing only one of the two statements. This question asks for the second law in general, and both statements together are the complete answer to that.

recall.must_convey: That the Clausius statement says heat does not flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter body, only when external work is done.
accept: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot
reject: cannot convert all the heat into work

steps.memory_tip: Clausius names the DIRECTION rule: cold to hot happens only with outside work.

steps.label: Kelvin-Planck statement
lines: in a cycle can take heat from a single
reservoir and convert all of it into work.
Some heat must always be rejected to a
steps.margin_note: Second mark. State that no engine converts heat from one reservoir completely into work.
steps.why: The first law alone does not forbid an engine that turns all its heat into work; the Kelvin-Planck statement is the separate rule that rules it out.
common_mistakes: Leaving out "working in a cycle". A single expansion can convert all its heat into work; a repeated cycle cannot.
Saying no heat can be converted into work at all. Part of the heat can become work; all of it cannot.

recall.must_convey: That the Kelvin-Planck statement says no engine working in a cycle can take heat from one reservoir and convert all of it into work.
accept: cannot convert all the heat into work
reject: heat cannot flow from a colder body to a hotter one

steps.memory_tip: Kelvin-Planck names the WORK rule: a single reservoir cannot supply an engine's work with nothing rejected.

insider_note: Both statements carry one mark each, so write both — the two together are the complete answer to this question.
